passage:
Dear Anjali,

At Nani's on Sunday, when Aunty said, "Why can't you be like Elizabeth?" I saw your face close, and I've felt bad ever since. I couldn't say anything in front of everyone.

So I'm saying it here. I'm not the perfect cousin they think I am. I nearly failed the physics test in November, and I cry in the bathroom before some exams. I hate being held up like a trophy, because then I can't tell anybody when things are hard.

Can we get chai this week, just us? I promise no marks talk, and I won't gloat. ❤️

Elizabeth

qa.q: Which subject did Elizabeth nearly fail in November?
qa.a: Elizabeth nearly failed the physics test.

qa.q: What is Elizabeth feeling about being held up as the ideal cousin?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels awkward and uncomfortable, unable to admit any struggles while held up on a pedestal.

qa.q: What could Elizabeth do to keep the friendship with Anjali steady?
qa.a: Elizabeth can stay kind, be honest about personal difficulties and avoid gloating, as the letter does by inviting Anjali for chai. ❤️

qa.q: How might Anjali feel when the aunt compares Anjali to Elizabeth?
qa.a: Probably small and stung, which is why Anjali's face closed, and Anjali may be envious without disliking Elizabeth.

grounding: Shows a teen cousin held up as ideal who writes kindly, admits their own difficulties and refuses to gloat.

passage:
Sudha, you asked why I never boast about your marks at family lunches. Let me tell you.
When I was fifteen, my Bua would point at me across the dinner mat and tell her son Manohar, "Look at Chetan, first in class. Why can't you be like him?" Everyone smiled at me. I wanted to sink into my plate. Nobody knew I was failing Hindi and crying over it at night.
One Diwali, Manohar muttered that I thought I was better than everyone. Part of me liked being the golden boy, I admit it. I could have smirked. Instead I followed him to the terrace and told him about my Hindi marks and my tutor's red ink. He stared, then laughed, and told me about his cricket trials. We stood there until the last rocket went up. Since that night, he has been my closest brother.

qa.q: Which subject was young Chetan failing?
How did young Chetan feel when Bua held him up as the example?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and lonely; he wanted to sink into his plate because nobody knew he was struggling, though part of him enjoyed the praise.

qa.q: What was the turning point on the terrace, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Chetan chose to admit his own Hindi struggles instead of smirking; that honesty took away the pedestal and let Manohar share his own story.

qa.q: How did Manohar probably see Chetan before the terrace talk?
qa.a: Manohar likely saw Chetan as a smug rival who thought he was better, because every family meal made Manohar look small next to him.

grounding: A cousin held up as the ideal feels awkward, refuses to gloat and admits his own difficulties to the cousin he was compared with.

passage:
The lights went out halfway through the sangeet. In the sudden dark, with the generator coughing and fifty relatives shouting for torches, Preeti heard her aunt again: "Lalit, just watch Preeti, na? School topper, still helps in the kitchen."
Preeti's cheeks went hot. She found Lalit on the back stairs, scrolling nothing on a dead phone.
"She says that every time," Lalit said flatly. "Enjoy it."
"I don't." Preeti sat a step below. "I failed my physics practical last month. I haven't told anyone. My hands shake before every test."
Lalit looked up. "You? Seriously?"
"Seriously. And I can't dance. You saw."
He snorted. The generator finally caught, and yellow light spilled over them.
"Don't tell Mausi," Preeti said.
"About the physics?"
"About the dancing." Lalit laughed properly this time, and the tight line in his jaw eased.

qa.q: What did Preeti fail last month?
Why did Preeti's cheeks go hot when her aunt praised her?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and uncomfortable being held up as perfect, knowing she had struggles nobody saw and that Lalit was hurt by the comparison.

qa.q: What small step helped Preeti and Lalit?
qa.a: Preeti admitted her failed practical and shaking hands instead of accepting the praise, which showed Lalit she was not above him.

qa.q: How does Lalit see the moment on the stairs?
qa.a: At first he feels bitter and expects Preeti to gloat; when she shares her failures he is surprised and relieved, and his jaw eases.

grounding: A teen held up as the ideal cousin feels awkward, refuses to enjoy the pedestal and shares her own difficulties during a power cut.
